"Then they found a servant from among Our servants, on whom We had bestowed mercy from Us, and whom We had taught knowledge from Us." The Qur'an leaves him unnamed — simply "a servant from among Our servants" — but Ibn Kathir affirms that this was al-Khidr, peace be upon him, as indicated by the authentic hadiths narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Indeed, the Bukhari narration opens with Ibn 'Abbas defending exactly this point: when Nawf al-Bikali claimed that the Musa of this story was not the Musa of the Children of Israel, Ibn 'Abbas said, "The enemy of Allah has told a lie," and cited the hadith of Ubayy bin Ka'b.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the name: al-Khadir literally means green, verdant, and the commentators at large say he was so named because wherever he sat, grass would spring up and the ground turn green, whatever the nature of the land.

The hadith paints the meeting. Back at the rock they found a man covered with a garment. Musa greeted him with salam, and he replied, "Is there such a greeting in your land?" — "I am Musa." — "The Musa of the Children of Israel?" — "Yes. I have come to you so that you may teach me something of that knowledge which you have been taught." And al-Khidr answered with the words the next ayah will record — "You will not be able to have patience with me" — adding: "O Musa, I have some of Allah's knowledge which He has bestowed upon me and you do not know it; and you have some of Allah's knowledge which He has bestowed upon you, and I do not know it."

Notice how ayah 65 itself frames al-Khidr's gifts: mercy "from Us" and knowledge taught "from Us". Nothing of it is presented as his own achievement; everything is attributed to Allah — the very point on which Musa had been corrected when he did not refer the knowledge back to Allah.

## Was al-Khidr a prophet?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Qur'an has not made it clear whether al-Khidr was a prophet or simply one of the men of Allah, and the question is treated in Tafsir al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr al-Muhit, and most commentaries. In the sight of the majority of religious scholars, however, the proof of his prophethood is embedded in the Qur'anic events themselves: what will issue from him later in this story runs outwardly counter to the Shari'ah, and no exemption from an injunction of the Shari'ah is possible except under the authority of divine revelation — something restricted to a prophet and messenger of Allah. A waliyy — a saintly "friend of Allah" — may receive kashf (illumination) or ilham (inspiration), but these can never establish a rule of the Law or change an injunction of the codified Shari'ah.

From this the Maʿārif draws a sharp practical warning: no waliyy anywhere in the world may be taken on the analogy of al-Khidr. The claim of some ignorant, misguided Sufis that "Tariqah" (the spiritual path) permits what the Shari'ah forbids — so that a "saint" seen openly committing a major sin may not be questioned — is flagrant, false heresy. Whatever al-Khidr did, he did under revealed divine authority, and no act contrary to the codified Shari'ah issuing from anyone else can be called permissible.

## Living the passage

Everything in these ayat models the manners of seeking knowledge. Musa — the prophet who spoke with Allah, superior in rank to the man he seeks — travels like an ardent student, endures fatigue, retraces his own steps, and asks to be taught. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that Allah had blessed him with such intense desire for knowledge that the mere scent of knowledge he did not possess set him travelling. The tests along the way — the vague address, the forgotten sign, the delayed hunger — teach that the road to knowledge is deliberately strewn with hardship, and that the seeker's setbacks may themselves be the signposts. And the passage closes where the search closes: at a rock the travellers had slept beside and walked past, with a servant of Allah whose mercy and knowledge the ayah attributes entirely to his Lord. The seeker's part was the searching, the stumbling, and the turning back; the finding, like the knowledge itself, was from Allah.

passages.title: Moses asks to follow and accepts the condition
passages.tafsir:
# The Adab of Seeking Knowledge — and Its Limits

This passage is the doorway into the famous journey of Mūsā (peace be upon him) with al-Khiḍr (upon him be peace). Mūsā asks — with striking humility — for permission to accompany him and learn; al-Khiḍr warns him twice that he will not be able to bear what he sees; Mūsā promises patience "if Allah wills"; and al-Khiḍr accepts him on one strict condition. What holds ayat 66–70 together is a single negotiation: the terms of companionship between two men who each carry a different kind of knowledge given by Allah.

## Two knowledges, both from Allah

Ibn Kathir opens his commentary on this passage with the key that unlocks everything that follows: al-Khiḍr (upon him be peace) "was one to whom Allah had given knowledge that He had not given to Mūsā, just as He had given Mūsā knowledge that He had not given to al-Khiḍr." Neither man is simply "above" the other. Each has a portion, and each has responsibilities before Allah that the other does not share.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (drawing on Tafsīr Mazharī of Qāḍī Thanāullah of Panipat) explains what this difference actually was. Prophets are generally sent with the mission of law and reform — a Book and a Sharīʿah, blueprints of guidance for people. But there is another category of divine work: the *takwīnī* imperatives, matters relating to the running of creation itself — that a certain person be saved from drowning, or another be removed. These are normally carried out by angels, but Allah chose some prophets for this service too, and al-Khiḍr (upon him be peace) was one of them. Abu Hayyan puts it concisely in al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ: the majority hold that al-Khiḍr was a prophet; his knowledge was of inner realities revealed to him, while the knowledge of Mūsā was of the injunctions and rulings on the apparent.

This is why, when the two knowledges seem to collide later in the story, there is no real contradiction. Certain specific events were exempted, by direct revelation, from the general rule of the Sharīʿah — and only the one appointed to carry them out knew it. The scholar of the law, judging by what is apparent, is *obliged* to call such an act unlawful; the one acting under the divine imperative is right in his own place. Both are obeying Allah.

## Ayah 66: how a seeker asks

"May I follow you, provided that you teach me something of what you have been taught?"

Ibn Kathir pauses over the wording. This is a question "phrased in gentle terms, with no sense of force or coercion" — and, he says, this is exactly how the seeker of knowledge should address the scholar. Notice each element:

- **"May I follow you" (hal attabiʿuka)** — a request for permission, not an announcement. And *attabiʿuka*, Ibn Kathir explains, means "I accompany you and spend time with you": Mūsā is not asking for a lecture but offering himself as a companion, ready to serve time and presence for the sake of learning.
- **"Something of what you have been taught" (mimmā ʿullimta)** — Mūsā acknowledges from the outset that al-Khiḍr's knowledge is itself a gift, taught to him by Allah, and asks only for a portion of it (*rushdan* — that by which he may be guided, learn something beneficial, and do righteous deeds).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the lesson explicitly, citing Qurtubi and Mazharī: here is Mūsā — a prophet and messenger of great resolve — most reverentially requesting to follow another man as his student. The etiquette of acquiring knowledge is that the student shows respect for the teacher and follows him as one eager to learn, **even if the student happens to be superior to his teacher**. Mūsā's rank did not exempt him from humility; it made his humility the more instructive.

## Ayat 67–68: the honest warning

Al-Khiḍr (upon him be peace) does not flatter his illustrious visitor. "You certainly cannot be patient with me" (ayah 67) — and then the reason (ayah 68): "How can you be patient with what your comprehension does not encompass?"

Ibn Kathir renders al-Khiḍr's meaning: you will see me doing things that go against your law, because I have knowledge from Allah that He has not taught you, and you have knowledge from Allah that He has not taught me. And — remarkably — al-Khiḍr concedes in advance that Mūsā's future objections will be *justified*: "I know that you will denounce me justifiably, but I have knowledge of Allah's wisdom and the hidden interests which I can see but you cannot." The problem is not a flaw in Mūsā; it is the structural impossibility of watching acts whose outward form violates the law you were sent to uphold, while their inner reality remains hidden from you.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens this into a principle: **it is not permissible for a scholar of the Sharīʿah to patiently bear what is contrary to the Sharīʿah.** When Mūsā later objects to what he sees, those objections will be "triggered by the dictates of his mission as a prophet" — they are not lapses of character but the duty of his office. No prophet can watch what appears to be a violation of Allah's law and maintain a stance of passive tolerance. Al-Khiḍr, knowing this, is telling Mūsā the truth about how the journey must go.

## Ayah 69: patience pledged — with "if Allah wills"

Mūsā answers: "You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter." Ibn Kathir explains the two halves: patience "with whatever I see of your affairs," and obedience — "I will not go against you in anything."

One thing in this pledge repays close attention: **why could Mūsā promise it at all?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the sharp question: if a scholar of the law may not promise to stay silent before violations of the law, how could Mūsā promise it? The answer given: Mūsā had been ordered to go and learn from al-Khiḍr (upon him be peace) *by none other than Allah Himself*. He was therefore at peace, trusting that nothing this man did would truly be counter to the Sharīʿah, however it might appear externally. On that basis the promise was sound — though, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, making such a promise would not be permissible for any ordinary scholar of the religion. And when Mūsā later did object, it was because his strong sense of honour for the Sharīʿah overtook him and he forgot the promise.

Notice, too, that Mūsā ties his pledge of patience to the will of Allah — "if Allah wills" — rather than resting it on his own strength.

## Ayah 70: the condition

Al-Khiḍr (upon him be peace) accepts, but sets a term: "Then if you follow me, do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you." Ibn Kathir explains: do not initiate any discussion of the matter — wait until I open it up, before you ask. The teacher reserves the right to choose the moment of explanation.

## The doctrinal safeguard: no one may imitate al-Khiḍr

Because this passage has historically been misused, the commentators close the door firmly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses that the exemption al-Khiḍr (upon him be peace) enjoyed could take effect **only through revelation to a prophet**. The *kashf* (illumination) or *ilhām* (inspiration) of a non-prophet — however saintly — can never lift a ruling of the Sharīʿah. To take the spiritual experiences of some non-prophet as analogous to al-Khiḍr, and thereby treat the unlawful as lawful — a notion popular among some ignorant Sufis — is, in the words of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, totally anti-religion and a rebellion against Islam.

The point is anchored in a striking exchange from the earliest generation. Ibn Abi Shaibah reports that Najdah al-Ḥarūrī, a Kharijite, wrote to Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) asking how al-Khiḍr could kill a minor boy when the Prophet ﷺ prohibited the killing of minors. Ibn ʿAbbās replied: if you were to receive the same knowledge about some minor as was received by Mūsā's "man of knowledge," the killing of a minor would become permissible for you too. His meaning: al-Khiḍr acted on revelation exclusive to a prophet — and since prophethood has ended with Muhammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ, the Last of the Prophets, no one after him can ever receive such a revelation. Hence the settled rule the commentary draws from the whole episode: no one other than a revelation-receiving prophet has the right to declare anyone exempted from any legal injunction of Islam.

## Living it

The passage models, in five short ayat, the whole etiquette of learning:

- **Ask permission gently.** Mūsā's "May I follow you?" — no force, no presumption — is, per Ibn Kathir, the template for how a seeker approaches a scholar.
- **Rank does not excuse you from humility.** If a messenger of great resolve could sit as a student, no one's credentials place them above learning from one whom Allah has taught something they lack.
- **Accept the teacher's terms.** Companionship in knowledge has conditions — here, restraint of the tongue until the teacher opens the matter.
- **Say "if Allah wills."** Mūsā attaches his promise of patience to Allah's will, not his own resolve.
- **Know the limits of the model.** Al-Khiḍr's case was unique — "there were prophets on both sides," as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it; therefore, the reality unfolded. It grants no license to anyone today to override the outward law on the strength of private inspiration.

passages.title: The ship, the boy, and the wall
passages.tafsir:
## Three tests, three questions, one parting

These ayat narrate the heart of the journey of Mūsā (peace be upon him) with al-Khiḍr: three episodes — a ship deliberately damaged, a boy killed, a wall repaired for free — each of which provokes Mūsā to object, until the third objection ends the companionship. What binds the ayat together is a single tension: Mūsā had agreed not to question anything al-Khiḍr did until al-Khiḍr himself explained it, and three times what he witnessed was so distressing that the agreement gave way. The passage is deliberately structured as a repetition — the same Arabic word *fa-nṭalaqā* ("so they set out," "so they proceeded," "so they moved on") opens each episode in ayat 71, 74, and 77 — so the reader feels the rhythm of test, protest, and reminder building toward the parting of ayah 78.

## The ship (ayat 71–73)

Ibn Kathir explains that the two set out having come to an agreement: al-Khiḍr's condition was that Mūsā should not ask about anything he found distasteful until al-Khiḍr initiated the explanation himself. Ibn Kathir then fills in the scene from the hadith: the crew of the ship recognised al-Khiḍr and let the two travellers board free of charge, as an honour to him. Once the boat was out at sea, far from shore, al-Khiḍr got up and damaged it — pulling out one of its planks and then patching it up again.

Mūsā, peace be upon him, could not restrain himself from denouncing him (ayah 71): "Have you damaged it wherein its people will drown? Verily, you have committed a thing *Imr*."

Two details in the Arabic repay attention:

**"That its people will drown" — consequence, not purpose.** Ibn Kathir notes that the grammatical structure of the sentence implies that drowning would be the *consequence* of the act, not al-Khiḍr's *purpose* in doing it. Mūsā is not accusing him of intending mass murder; he is pointing at where the act, on its face, leads.

**The word *Imr*.** Ibn Kathir records two readings from the early authorities: Mujāhid said it means "an evil thing," while Qatādah said "an astounding thing." Either way, it is a word of strong denunciation — Mūsā sees something that looks both shocking and wrong.

Al-Khiḍr's reply in ayah 72 is not an explanation but a reminder of the contract: "Did I not tell you, that you would not be able to have patience with me?" — meaning, as Ibn Kathir paraphrases, "this thing that I did deliberately is one of the things I told you not to denounce me for, because you do not know the full story, and there is a reason and purpose for it that you do not know about."

Mūsā's answer in ayah 73 is a model of humility from a great prophet: "Call me not to account for what I forgot, and be not hard upon me for my affair (with you)" — meaning, as Ibn Kathir glosses, "do not be harsh with me." Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on this very verse: "In the first instance, Mūsā asked al-Khiḍr because he had forgotten his promise." The first lapse, then, was genuine forgetfulness — not defiance.

**Did the ship actually sink?** Maarif ul Quran addresses the obvious worry. It notes that in the hadith of the Ṣaḥīḥs of al-Bukhārī and Muslim, al-Khiḍr dislodged a plank of the boat with an axe, creating a real danger that water would fill it and it would capsize — which is precisely why Mūsā objected. Yet according to historical reports the water never did fill the boat. Maarif offers two possibilities: either al-Khiḍr repaired it himself soon after — a report carried by al-Baghawī says he replaced the plank with glass — or the water was simply held back miraculously. And, it adds, the Qur'an's own context tells us the boat did not capsize, which supports these reports. The damage, in other words, was calibrated: enough to achieve its (as yet hidden) purpose, never enough to destroy the people aboard.

## The boy (ayat 74–76)

The second test is far harsher. Ibn Kathir relates that the boy was playing with other boys in one of the towns, and that al-Khiḍr deliberately singled him out — he was the finest and most handsome of them all — and killed him. If the first act merely *threatened* life, this one took it. So Mūsā's denunciation in ayah 74 is, as Ibn Kathir says, even more fervent than the first, and spoken hastily: "Have you killed an innocent person without *Nafs*? Verily, you have committed a thing *Nukr*!"

Again the vocabulary carries the weight:

**"An innocent person" — *nafsan zakiyyah*.** Maarif ul Quran draws out why this phrase matters. The word *ghulām* in Arabic usage denotes a minor boy, and Ibn ʿAbbās and most commentators corroborate that this boy was indeed a minor. The description *zakiyyah* — "free of sin" — supports it, because such a description fits only a prophet or a minor child, one who faces no accounting for his deeds and against whom no sin is written in his Book of Deeds. The Qur'an's own wording thus insists on exactly what makes the act so incomprehensible: this was a child with a clean record.

**"Without *Nafs*."** Ibn Kathir explains: there was no reason for killing him at all that Mūsā could see.

**From *Imr* to *Nukr*.** Where the first act was *Imr* (shocking, grievous), this one is *Nukr* — which Ibn Kathir glosses as "something that is clearly evil." The escalation in Mūsā's language mirrors the escalation of the deed.

Al-Khiḍr responds in ayah 75 with the same reminder as before — "Did I not tell you that you can have no patience with me?" — reiterating, as Ibn Kathir says, the condition set in the first place. And this time Mūsā, knowing he has used up his excuses, sets his own terminus in ayah 76: "If I ask you anything after this, keep me not in your company, you have received an excuse from me" — meaning, as Ibn Kathir paraphrases, "if I object to anything else you do after this," for "you have accepted my apology twice."

Here Ibn Kathir records a moving report: Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that Ubayy bin Kaʿb said: whenever the Prophet ﷺ mentioned anyone, he would pray for himself first. One day he said: "May the mercy of Allah be upon us and upon Mūsā. If he had stayed with his companion he would have seen wonders, but he said, 'If I ask you anything after this, keep me not in your company, you have received an excuse from me.'" The Prophet's ﷺ words carry a gentle wistfulness: patience under what we cannot yet understand opens doors onto wonders; impatience — however understandable — closes them.

## The wall (ayat 77–78)

The third episode inverts the moral puzzle. In the first two, al-Khiḍr seemed to do harm without cause; now he does good without reward — and to people who deserve none. The two travellers come to a town whose people, in the words of the hadith Ibn Kathir cites, were mean — that is, miserly. Mūsā and al-Khiḍr asked them for food, and they refused to host them. Then, in that very town, they found a wall on the point of collapse, and al-Khiḍr set it up straight. Ibn Kathir notes from the hadith that he did this with his own hands, supporting it until it stood upright again — something extraordinary in itself.

**Which town was it?** Ibn Kathir records that Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn Sīrīn that it was al-Aylah. Maarif ul Quran gathers the reports: Antakiah according to Ibn ʿAbbās, Aikah according to Ibn Sīrīn, and — in a report from Abū Hurayrah cited via Mazhari — some habitation of al-Andulus (Spain); it closes, as one must with such differences, "Allah knows best." The Qur'an itself leaves the town nameless, and the story loses nothing by it.

Mūsā's third remark is the mildest of the three — not an accusation of wrongdoing but a suggestion: "If you had wished, surely you could have taken wages for it!" (ayah 77). Ibn Kathir unpacks the logic: since these people refused us even the hospitality of guests, why labour for them for free? It is a reasonable observation — and that is precisely the point. Even Mūsā's most measured, most justified-sounding question still counts as a question, and by his own stipulation in ayah 76 it ends the journey.

So al-Khiḍr says (ayah 78): "This is the parting between you and I" — because, as Ibn Kathir explains, Mūsā had himself said after the boy was killed that one more question would end the companionship; "so this is the parting of the ways between me and you." But the parting is not a door slammed shut: "I will tell you the interpretation (*taʾwīl*) — meaning the explanation, as Ibn Kathir glosses it — "of (those) things over which you were not able to be patient." The hidden wisdom Mūsā could not wait for is about to be disclosed, and the ayat that follow will supply it.

## Reading the three tests together

Set side by side, the three episodes form a graded sequence. The first act threatened the lives of a boatful of people; the second took the life of a sinless child; the third was merely unpaid labour for miserly hosts. Mūsā's responses trace the same arc in reverse: a horrified denunciation, an even more fervent one, then a mild suggestion about wages. Yet all three spring from the same source — distress at acts whose justification lay entirely out of view. Al-Khiḍr never argues the merits of any deed; each time he simply repeats the one thing Mūsā actually needs to hear: *you do not know the full story*. As Ibn Kathir puts it, there was "a reason and purpose for it that you do not know about."

The passage does not ask believers to suspend moral judgment — the Prophet ﷺ himself invoked Allah's mercy upon Mūsā, coupling his name with our own. What it dramatises is the narrow, painful space between what we see and what Allah knows, and the discipline — *ṣabr*, patience, the word repeated in ayat 72, 75, and 78 — required to hold that space open. And it offers a quiet consolation for our failures in it: even when patience runs out, the explanation still comes. The parting of ayah 78 is not the end of the story but the threshold of its meaning.

passages.title: The hidden wisdom behind the three deeds
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are the unveiling. For three stages of the journey, Musa (peace be upon him) watched al-Khidr do things that looked indefensible — scuttling a boat, killing a boy, rebuilding a wall for nothing in return — and his sense of justice could not stay silent. Now, at the moment of parting, al-Khidr explains each deed, and the passage closes with the words that hold the whole story together: "I did them not of my own accord… That is the interpretation of those things over which you could not be patient" (ayah 82). As Ibn Kathir puts it, this is the explanation of what Musa found so hard to understand and openly condemned: Allah had shown al-Khidr the hidden reasons behind each apparent wrong.

## Ayah 79 — the damaged boat that stayed afloat

The boat belonged to *masakin* — poor people who worked at sea. Ibn Kathir relays al-Khidr's own reasoning: ahead of them lay a king who "seized every boat by force" — that is, every *good, sound* boat. By making the vessel appear faulty, al-Khidr made it worthless in the tyrant's eyes, so that its poor owners — who had nothing else — could keep it and go on benefiting from it. Some said the owners were orphans. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the report of Kaʿb al-Ahbar that they were ten brothers: five handicapped, and five who worked the boat to feed them all — a detail that sharpens how much hung on that one hull. Al-Baghawi reports from Ibn ʿAbbas that the cruel king lay in the very direction the boat was sailing; al-Khidr pulled out a plank so that the king, seeing a damaged boat, would let it go — the "damage" was a rescue timed exactly.

**A legal insight hidden in one word.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazhari) draws a definition of *miskin* from this verse. These people owned a boat — property worth no less than the *nisab*, the minimum wealth at which zakah becomes due — yet the Qurʼan still calls them *masakin*. So a miskin is not only someone with nothing at all: whoever lacks wealth beyond his basic, necessary needs up to the nisab threshold is included, because these owners' boat was itself engaged in earning their bare necessities.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes the sage Rumi's couplet on this scene: yes, al-Khidr broke the boat at sea — but in that one breaking "a hundred saving graces" can be seen.

## Ayat 80–81 — the boy, and the mercy folded inside grief

This is the deed that tested Musa most, and the sources dwell on it. Al-Khidr explains that the boy's parents were believers, "and we feared he would oppress them by rebellion and disbelief." Ibn Kathir records the hadith — narrated by Ibn ʿAbbas from Ubayy bin Kaʿb, and recorded by Ibn Jarir — that the Prophet ﷺ said the boy al-Khidr killed "was destined to be a disbeliever from the day he was created." The fear in ayah 80 was not merely that he would grieve his parents: their very *love* for him might make them follow him into disbelief. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same — grown into an infidel, he would be a living trial for his parents and a danger to their faith itself.

**Qatadah's meditation on the decree.** Ibn Kathir quotes Qatadah: the parents rejoiced when he was born and grieved when he was killed — yet had he lived, he would have been the cause of their doom. "So let a man be content with the decree of Allah, for the decree of Allah for the believer, if he dislikes it, is better for him than if He were to decree something that he likes for him." Ibn Kathir supports this with an authentic hadith — that Allah does not decree anything for the believer except that it is good for him — and with the ayah: "it may be that you dislike a thing which is good for you" (2:216). This is the beating heart of the whole passage: what looks like pure loss from inside a moment can be pure mercy from above it.

**"Better in righteousness and nearer to mercy."** In ayah 81, al-Khidr says they wished that the Lord of the parents would give them a replacement better in purity (*zakah*) and closer in compassion. Ibn Jurayj explained: a child better than this one, for whom they would feel more compassion. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses it as one better in deeds and morals and more devoted to fulfilling the parents' due rights, and adds the report — carried by Ibn Abi Shaibah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim from Ibn ʿAtiyyah — that Allah blessed the couple with a *girl* in the boy's place, who became the mother of a prophet; a report from Ibn ʿAbbas says she gave birth to two prophets, and other reports say that through the prophet she bore, Allah guided a large community. The replacement was not merely "another child" but generations of guidance.

**Did the killing contradict Allah's knowledge?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious objection: if Allah knew the boy would become a disbeliever, must that not have come to pass, since nothing can occur contrary to divine knowledge? The answer (from Mazhari) is that the divine knowledge carried a condition: *if he reached maturity*, he would not only disbelieve himself but pose a danger to other Muslims. Since he was killed before maturity, nothing occurred contrary to Allah's knowledge. And who "feared" and "intended" in the plural — "we feared… we intended"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two readings: al-Khidr was attributing the apprehension and wish to himself and Allah together; or to himself alone, in which case "we intended" means "we prayed to Allah" — since exchanging a child for a better one belongs exclusively to Allah, and no human being can be associated with it.

## Ayah 82 — the wall, the treasure, and a righteous father

The wall belonged to two orphan boys of the town, and beneath it lay a treasure that was theirs. ʿIkrimah, Qatadah and others said it was wealth buried for them — the meaning Ibn Kathir says is apparent from the context and was chosen by Ibn Jarir. So al-Khidr repaired the wall — for no charge, as Ibn Kathir's heading notes — so that the boys could reach "their full strength" and take out their treasure themselves. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records two reports on the treasure: Abu al-Dardaʼ reported from the Prophet ﷺ that it was a treasure chest of gold and silver (narrated by Tirmidhi and al-Hakim, as cited from Mazhari); and Ibn ʿAbbas said it was a tablet of gold inscribed with good counsel — opening with the Basmalah and closing with the testimony of faith — each line marvelling at the human contradiction: how can one who believes in destiny despair? how can one who believes in the Reckoning of the Hereafter stay heedless?

**"And their father was a righteous man."** Ibn Kathir draws the great lesson: a righteous person's offspring are taken care of; the blessing of his worship extends to them in this world and the Hereafter — through his intercession for them and their being raised to the highest levels of Paradise — as stated in the Qurʼan and reported in the Sunnah. Saʿid bin Jubayr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: the boys were taken care of *because their father was righteous* — it is not even stated that the boys themselves were. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the treasure was secured through al-Khidr because the father was a pious man dear in the sight of Allah; Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir (cited from Mazhari) said: because of the piety and righteousness of one servant, Allah protects his children, his children's children, his family, even the homes built around his own. Al-Qurtubi relates that the sage Shibli used to say he was a guarantee of peace for his city and its surroundings; soon after his death, the disbelievers of Dailam crossed the Euphrates and took Baghdad. Mazhari adds a social corollary: people, too, should show consideration and affection to the children of the learned and the pious — unless those children fall into disbelief and sin.

**"Their full strength" (ashudd).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *ashudd* as full maturity — the age at which a person becomes able to decide what is good or bad for him. Imam Abu Hanifah put it at twenty-five years; others said forty, citing "until, when he reaches his maturity and reaches forty years" (46:15).

**A note on wording.** Ibn Kathir observes that ayah 82 calls the place *al-madinah* (the city) while ayah 77 had called it a *qaryah* (village/town) — proof that *qaryah* in the Qurʼan can denote a city, as in 47:13 and 43:31.

## "I wished… we intended… your Lord willed" — the etiquette of speaking about Allah

Both commentaries pause over a stunning pattern in al-Khidr's speech. For the boat — an act that outwardly looked like pure damage — he said *aradtu*, "**I** wished to damage it" (ayah 79). For the boy — where killing was an apparent evil but the promised replacement a pure good — he said *aradna*, "**we** intended" (ayah 81), the plural letting the evil face toward himself and the good toward Allah. For the wall — an act of unmixed good to orphans — he said *fa-arada rabbuka*, "**your Lord** intended" (ayah 82), attributing it entirely to Allah; and, as Ibn Kathir notes, no one but Allah is able to bring two children to the age of full strength.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the theology beneath this. Nothing, good or apparent evil, happens without the will and intention of Allah; and in terms of the total, wisdom-based order of His creation, no evil is truly evil. Yet *adab* — reverent etiquette — demands that evil not be verbally attributed to Allah. The model is Ibrahim (peace be upon him) in the Qurʼan: "It is He who gives me to eat and drink, and *when I am sick*, it is He who cures me" (26:79–80) — feeding and curing attributed to Allah, sickness attributed to himself. Al-Khidr's three verbs are a wordless lesson in the same courtesy.

## Was al-Khidr a prophet — and who was he?

"It was a mercy from your Lord, and I did them not of my own accord" (ayah 82). Ibn Kathir reads this as proof, for those who hold that view, that al-Khidr (peace be upon him) was a prophet: he acted only by command enjoined upon him — alongside 18:65, which says Allah had bestowed mercy on him from Himself and taught him knowledge from His own presence. His very name carries a sign. Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said that the Prophet ﷺ said concerning al-Khidr: "He was called Al-Khidr because he sat on a barren Farwah that turned white, then it turned green beneath him." And Sahih al-Bukhari records, from Hammam from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "He was called Al-Khidr because he sat on a barren Farwah and it turned green beneath him." As for the word *farwah* itself, Ibn Kathir notes that in ʿAbdur-Razzaq's view it means a patch of withered vegetation; it was also said to mean the face of the earth. Al-Khidr means "the Green One" — the very ground beneath him bore witness.

Is al-Khidr still alive? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān surveys the dispute honestly: some reports suggest he is alive and others tell otherwise, and scholarly opinion has always been at variance. In Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit, Abu Hasan has reported events of several pious elders having met al-Khidr, yet also states that the majority of religious scholars hold that he has died. Qadi Thanaʼullah of Panipati favoured the resolution attributed to Sayyid Ahmad al-Sarhandi. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's conclusion is the soundest guidance: no article of faith or religious practice depends on this question, the Qurʼan and Sunnah give no clear statement on it, and we are not obligated to believe either side — so there is no need to enter into debate over it.

## Two last subtleties

**A softened verb.** Ibn Kathir notices that in ayah 78 al-Khidr said "what you were *not able* (lam tastatiʿ) to bear patiently," but here in ayah 82, once everything was explained, he used the shorter, milder form *lam tastiʿ* — "what you *could not* bear patiently." The intensity of the verbal form reflects the intensity of the confusion felt; once the knots were untied, the language itself relaxed. The Qurʼan makes the same distinction in 18:97 about the barrier of Yaʼjuj and Maʼjuj: they "were not able to scale it" — in the lighter form — "nor are they able to dig through it" — in the heavier form, for digging through is harder than climbing over.

**The forgotten companion.** If one asks what became of Musa's young servant from the start of the story, Ibn Kathir answers: the story's objective is what passed between Musa and al-Khidr; the servant was simply with Musa, following him — and the Sahih hadiths identify him as Yushaʿ bin Nun, who became the leader of the Children of Israel after Musa (peace be upon him).

## Living it

The passage does not license anyone to imitate al-Khidr — he acted, as he says, not of his own accord but by Allah's command and mercy. What it gives the believer is a way of seeing. The broken boat, the buried child, the wall rebuilt for no charge: each was mercy wearing the mask of misfortune. So, in Qatadah's words, let a person be content with the decree of Allah — what He decrees for the believer, even when disliked, is better than what the believer would have chosen. And let parents take the quiet promise of ayah 82 to heart: righteousness is an inheritance. A father's piety guarded a treasure under a leaning wall long after he was gone; what a believer's worship banks for his children may be worth more than anything he leaves in his will.

# Dhul-Qarnayn: The Question That Was Meant to Be a Test (18:83–88)

This passage turns to Dhul-Qarnayn, a righteous and just king whom Allah established in the earth and equipped with the means to reach its farthest limits. Ayat 83–84 set out his commission — the question put to the Prophet ﷺ and the divine empowerment that made this king what he was — and ayat 85–88 recount the first leg of his journey, to the far west, where his justice and faith are put on display in the ruling he gives over a people he finds there. What binds the six ayat together is a single idea: worldly power placed in the hands of a believer, and used exactly as Allah intends.

## The question behind the question

Ayah 83 begins, "They ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn." Who was asking, and why? Ibn Kathir explains that the disbelievers of Makkah had sent word to the People of the Book, seeking material with which they could test the Prophet ﷺ. The reply came back: ask him about a man who travelled extensively throughout the earth, about some young men whose fate nobody knows, and about the Rūḥ (the soul) — and Sūrat al-Kahf was revealed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, relates that it was the Quraysh of Makkah who asked, coached to put three questions to the Prophet ﷺ in order to test his prophethood and veracity. Two of the three had already been answered: the story of the People of the Cave earlier in this very sūrah (ayat 9–26), and the question about the Rūḥ towards the end of the previous sūrah (17:85). Who was Dhul-Qarnayn? — this is the third.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests there may have been a deeper reason this particular question was chosen. It is likely, the author writes, that among the questions the Jews of Madinah had set for the Quraysh of Makkah to test his prophethood was this question about Dhul-Qarnayn, and that it carried an underlying purpose: this question was special, since the Jews took him to be their savior and respected him. On the research the author cites, Dhul-Qarnayn may have been that very king — the righteous ruler who confronted Nebuchadnezzar, secured the release of the Bani Isrāʼīl from captivity, resettled them in Palestine, and had the treasures of Baytul-Maqdis returned to them. A question about a figure they revered would be a searching test of a man claiming revelation.

And the answer satisfied them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that after the Qur'anic reply the questioners asked nothing further — not his name's origin, his country, or his era — which tells us even they treated such details as unnecessary.

## "Something of his story" — a grammatical signal

The wording of ayah 83 repays attention. The Prophet ﷺ is told to say, "I shall recite to you *minhu dhikrā*" — literally, "some mention *of* him" — rather than the shorter *dhikrahu*, "his story." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why: the particle *min* ("some of") and the indefinite form of *dhikrā* (marked by the tanwīn, the Arabic indefinite ending) are deliberate indicators. The Qur'an is announcing in advance that it will not narrate the whole story of Dhul-Qarnayn in its historical setting; it will relate only a part — the part that carries guidance. Everything else — his name, lineage, country, century — the Qur'an has consciously skipped as unnecessary.

This is why the commentators' honest position on his identity matters. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān surveys the views: Ibn Kathir, in al-Bidāyah wa an-Nihāyah, placed him in the era of Ibrāhīm عليه السلام — reporting from the early righteous elders that Dhul-Qarnayn travelled on foot for Hajj, that Ibrāhīm عليه السلام went out of Makkah to greet him, prayed for him and counselled him, and (as reported from Adhraqi) performed tawāf with him. Al-Bairūnī identified him as a Himyarite king of Yemen — and Ibn Kathir also relates the view that he was the first Tubbaʻ of Yemen. Maulana Hifzur-Rahman, in Qaṣaṣ al-Qurʼān, argued for the Persian king known as Khorus to the Jews, Cyrus to the Greeks, and Kai-Khusro to the Arabs, of the era of the prophet Dāniyāl. The one identification the sources firmly reject is the most popular one: Alexander the Macedonian, who had Aristotle as his minister and lived some three hundred years before Sayyidnā Masīḥ عليه السلام. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — presenting the research of Ibn Kathir in al-Bidāyah wa an-Nihāyah — calls this identification totally wrong: that Alexander was a fire-worshipping polytheist, whereas the Dhul-Qarnayn of the Qur'an was, by unanimous agreement and by the Qur'an's own testimony, a righteous believer, and the two were separated by more than two thousand years. The misconception has been persistent, Maʿārif notes — even commentators of the stature of Abū Ḥayyān in al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ and al-Ālūsī in Rūḥ al-Maʿānī identified the Qur'anic Dhul-Qarnayn with him.

As for the name itself — "the possessor of two horns" — the sayings differ widely: two locks of hair, rule over East and West, marks or wounds on the two sides of his head, or (as Ibn Kathir mentions) that he reached the two "horns" of the sun, its rising and setting points. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the Qur'an never gave him this name at all; it came from the Jews, and he may have been known by it among them. And the author's closing counsel is worth taking to heart: what the Qur'an did not claim and no authentic hadith explained, we are not obligated to settle. The Ṣaḥābah and Tābiʻīn paid these details no particular attention, and whichever historical view proves weightiest, the Qur'an's purpose stands achieved either way.

Was he a prophet? Here the scholars genuinely differed. Ibn Kathir inclined to the view that he was; the majority hold, on the report from ʻAlī ؓ transmitted through Abi al-Tufayl, that he was neither prophet nor angel but a righteous believing servant. The question resurfaces below at ayah 86.

## Empowerment from Allah, not from himself (ayah 84)

"Surely We established him in the land, and gave him the means (*sabab*) of everything." Notice the grammar of grace: *We* established him, *We* gave him. Ibn Kathir explains the establishment as comprehensive kingly power — armies, war equipment, siege machinery — such that east and west submitted to him and nations Arab and non-Arab served him; and he compares the phrasing to what was said of Bilqīs, "she has been given all things" (27:23), meaning all that monarchs of her kind are given.

The key word is *sabab*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, defines it as anything harnessed to achieve an objective — material instruments and resources, but also knowledge, insight and experience. Ibn Kathir records that Ibn ʻAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʻīd bin Jubayr, ʻIkrimah, As-Suddī, Qatādah and Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk all glossed it as *knowledge*, while Qatādah also said it means knowledge of the parts and features of the earth. So Dhul-Qarnayn was no mere conqueror with a large army: he was equipped with everything a just ruler needs — power *and* understanding — "to maintain his just rule, establish universal peace," as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, and to humble the people of shirk (associating partners with Allah).

## The westward journey (ayat 85–86)

"So he followed a way" (ayah 85). Ibn ʻAbbās said he pursued the various routes to achieve his aims; Mujāhid, that he took the routes east and west; Qatādah, that he followed the routes and landmarks of the earth. The point Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds is subtle: though Allah had given him means to *every* region, the first use he made of them was to travel west — the account of his journeys begins here.

Ayah 86: "until he reached the setting-place of the sun, and found it setting in a spring of *ḥamiʼah*." Two clarifications from the sources prevent misreading.

**First, the "setting-place."** Ibn Kathir is unambiguous: this means the furthest point that can be reached in the direction of sunset — the west of the earth — not some place in the sky where the sun literally goes down. The storytellers' tales of a man who travelled so far that the sun set *behind* him Ibn Kathir dismisses flatly as impossible and untrue, mostly drawn from the myths of the People of the Book and the fabrications and lies of their heretics. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: he reached the western limit beyond which there was no populated area.

**Second, the "spring of ḥamiʼah."** The word derives (on one of two views Ibn Kathir mentions) from *ḥamaʼah*, mud — the same root as the "altered mud" from which Adam was created in 15:28. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it as water over dark mud, making the water itself appear black — a dark, miry spring. And the sun "setting in" it is the language of appearance, not astronomy. Ibn Kathir gives the perfect everyday analogy: anyone standing on a coast sees the sun apparently sinking into the sea, yet the sun never leaves its fixed course. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers the parallel of an open plain at sunset — with no mountain, tree or building on the horizon, the eye naturally reads the sun as sinking into the land. The Qur'an narrates what Dhul-Qarnayn *found* — what the scene looked like from where he stood at the world's western edge — with perfect precision.

## "We said: O Dhul-Qarnayn" — who spoke, and how?

Near that spring "he found a people" — Ibn Kathir notes they were said to be a great nation of the children of Adam, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān infers from what follows that they were disbelievers. Then comes a striking sentence: "*We said*: O Dhul-Qarnayn! Either you punish them, or take a way of kindness among them."

Allah Himself addresses him. How? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the possibilities. If Dhul-Qarnayn was a prophet, the address is straightforward revelation (*waḥy*). If not, either the address reached him through a prophet of his time — and the reported presence of al-Khaḍir عليه السلام with him suggests exactly this — or it was inspiration in the broader, non-prophetic sense, like Allah's word to the mother of Mūsā عليه السلام, "We inspired her" (*awḥaynā*), though she was no prophet. But Abu Ḥayyān in al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ presses a sharper point: the address here contains an authorization to punish, even to kill — and no such command can rest on mystical unveiling (*kashf*) or inspiration (*ilhām*); it requires true revelation to a prophet. Hence only two positions remain sound: either Dhul-Qarnayn was himself a prophet, or a prophet stood beside him through whom the address came. And Allah knows best.

## The ruling that revealed the man (ayat 87–88)

Allah gave him unchecked power over that nation and a genuine choice. Ibn Kathir spells out how wide the choice was: he could have killed the men and taken the women and children captive, or freed them with or without ransom. "His justice and faith became apparent," Ibn Kathir says, "in the ruling he pronounced."

That ruling is a model of just governance, and it divides cleanly in the two ayat:

**"As for him who does wrong, we shall punish him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment" (ayah 87).** The "wrong" (*ẓulm*) here, Ibn Kathir explains, is persisting in disbelief and in associating partners with Allah — and Qatādah glossed the worldly punishment as killing. But note the sequence Dhul-Qarnayn himself articulates: his own punishment is limited and worldly; the *terrible* punishment belongs to Allah in the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir observes that this very sentence is a confirmation of the Hereafter and of reward and punishment — from the lips of an ancient king. His power never deluded him into thinking judgment ended with his own court.

**"And as for him who believes and does righteousness, he shall have the finest reward, and we shall speak to him from our command with ease" (ayah 88).** The believer — one who, in Ibn Kathir's words, follows the call to worship Allah alone with no partner — receives the best reward in the Hereafter with Allah, and from Dhul-Qarnayn himself gentle treatment: Mujāhid explained the "easy words" as words of kindness.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses that offered the two options, Dhul-Qarnayn *chose the second* — benevolence first. He would not punish anyone before calling them: he undertook to bring the people to the straight path through good counsel and the spreading of the message, and only then reward the believers and punish those who clung to disbelief. Power in his hands opened with daʻwah, not the sword.

## What the passage leaves with us

This passage is a portrait of power in the hands of a believer. Dhul-Qarnayn is what the tyrant is not: given the means of everything, the Qur'an insists it was Allah who established him and Allah who gave; given absolute discretion over a conquered people, he begins with kindness and counsel; given the sword, he wields it only against persistent wrong, and even then he defers the real reckoning to "his Lord." The Qur'an, which tells us it is giving only "some mention of him," has told us exactly the part worth knowing: not where he ruled or when, but *how* — and that a believer entrusted with the earth answers to the One who established him in it.

passages.title: The eastward journey to an exposed people
