# The Eastward Journey to an Exposed People (18:89–91)

This short passage is the second leg of Dhul-Qarnayn's great journey. Ibn Kathir tells us that he now travelled from the west of the earth towards the east — to the place of the sun's rising — where he finds a people living utterly exposed, with nothing between them and the sun. The three ayat form one tight unit: the setting out (ayah 89), the arrival and the strange people found there (ayah 90), and Allah's closing comment that His knowledge encompassed everything about this king and his far-flung expedition (ayah 91).

## Ayah 89: another way, the same mission

Ayah 89 — "Then he travelled a different course" (thumma atbaʿa sababan) — turns the story in a new direction: having been in the west, Dhul-Qarnayn now sets out along another route, this time toward the east.

Ibn Kathir fills in what the terse ayah implies about the character of this march. Dhul-Qarnayn travelled from the west of the earth toward the east, and every time he passed a nation he subjugated its people and **called them to Allah**. If they obeyed him, all well and good; otherwise he would humiliate them and take their wealth and possessions, and from every nation he took what his armies needed to fight the next. The picture is of conquest in the service of daʿwah (calling people to Allah), not plunder for its own sake — at every nation along the road, power is harnessed to the summons to worship Allah.

## Ayah 90: a people with no shelter against the sun

At the "rising place of the sun" — the easternmost reach of his journey — he finds the sun "rising on a people for whom We had provided no shelter against the sun." Ibn Kathir explains the phrase simply: they had no buildings and no trees to cover them and shade them from the sun's heat. They lived on open ground under the full force of the sky.

The early authority Qatadah gives a vivid report of how such a life was possible: "It was mentioned to us that they were in a land where nothing grew, so when the sun rose they would go into tunnels until it had passed its zenith, then they would come out to go about their daily lives and earn themselves a living." A barren land, no timber to build with, no vegetation for shade — so the people burrowed beneath the earth through the fiercest hours and emerged in the afternoon to work.

Notice how the ayah words this: it is *Allah* who says "We had provided no shelter for them" (lam najʿal lahum min dūnihā sitran). Even the strange condition of this remote nation is framed as Allah's own doing — He is the One who did not appoint shelter for them, so their exposed life is described from the first as lying within His arrangement of the world.

## What the Qur'an leaves unsaid — and why

A reader naturally asks: what did Dhul-Qarnayn *do* with these people? What was their religion? Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to a subtle feature of the passage. The Qur'an describes the people's outward state — that they were not accustomed to the ways and means of protection against the sun, such as houses, tents, and dress — but it says nothing about their faith and deeds, and nothing about what Dhul-Qarnayn did to them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, as in al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ) explains the silence: it is obvious that these people too were disbelievers, and Dhul-Qarnayn handled them the way he had handled the people he had found in the west, mentioned earlier in the surah. Describing it again here was simply not considered necessary, because the reader can work it out on the analogy of the previous event.

## Ayah 91: "And We truly had full knowledge of him"

The passage closes with a compressed divine comment: "So it was. And We truly had full knowledge of him" (kadhālika wa-qad aḥaṭnā bimā ladayhi khubran). "So it was" — the matter was just as described — and then the weightier clause: Allah knew all about Dhul-Qarnayn.

Mujahid and As-Suddi explain: Allah knew everything about him and his army, and nothing was hidden from Him, even though they came from so many different nations and lands — and they cite the ayah, "Truly, nothing is hidden from Allah, in the earth or in the heaven" (3:5). Think of what this comment is doing at this point in the story. Dhul-Qarnayn has now stood at both extremities of the inhabited earth, commanding armies drawn from many peoples. From a human vantage point, no career could be vaster. Yet the whole of it — every soldier from every land, every route taken, every people encountered, including a nation so obscure it lived in tunnels in a land where nothing grew — lay fully within Allah's knowledge. The greatest of kings and the remotest of peoples are alike known to Him: nothing in the earth or the heaven is hidden from Allah.

## Taking it to heart

Two threads are worth carrying away. First, Dhul-Qarnayn's consistency: as Ibn Kathir describes, at every nation along his eastward march he called the people to Allah, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes that he dealt with the people of the east just as he had dealt with those of the west. Righteous use of power is a pattern, not a one-off performance. Second, ayah 91 quietly re-frames the entire epic. However far a person travels and however much he commands, he moves entirely within the compass of Allah's knowledge. For the believer that is both a caution — nothing we do is hidden — and a comfort: no people is so remote, and no life so exposed, that it falls outside the knowledge of Allah, for truly nothing is hidden from Him in the earth or in the heaven.

passages.title: The plea for a barrier against Gog and Magog
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat open the final scene of Dhul-Qarnayn's story: his third great journey ends at a mountain pass where a helpless, isolated people beg him to wall out two nations of destroyers — Ya'juj and Ma'juj (Gog and Magog). What binds the passage together is a single movement: the journey (ayah 92), the arrival at the pass and the meeting with its people (ayah 93), and their plea and offer of payment (ayah 94). Everything that follows — the building of the great barrier — grows out of this request.

## The third journey and the two mountains

Ayah 92 repeats the refrain that structures the whole narrative: *thumma atbaʿa sababan* — "then he followed another way." Ibn Kathir explains that Dhul-Qarnayn now travelled from the east of the earth until he reached a place between two mountains standing next to one another with a valley in between — the very gap from which Ya'juj and Ma'juj would emerge into the land of the Turks to spread mischief, destroying crops and people.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note on the people Dhul-Qarnayn had just left behind in the east — those living exposed to the sun. The Qur'an says nothing about their faith or about what he did among them; but, citing al-Bahr al-Muhit from Ibn 'Atiyyah, it observes that we may reasonably conclude he dealt with them just as he had dealt with the people of the west, and the Qur'an simply did not need to repeat itself.

## Between the two barriers (ayah 93)

In ayah 93 the key word is *as-saddayn*, "the two barriers." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that a *sadd* is anything that blocks — it may be a wall or a mountain, natural or man-made. Here it means the two mountains that already stood as a natural barrier against Ya'juj and Ma'juj. The problem was the pass between them: the raiders still attacked through that gap, and it was this opening that Dhul-Qarnayn would later close.

There he found "a people who scarcely understood a word." Ibn Kathir explains this simply: he could not understand their speech, because they were so isolated from other people. The detail matters — it paints a community at the edge of the known world, without language in common with anyone, without power, and squarely in the path of the most destructive nations on earth.

## The plea and the offer of tribute (ayah 94)

Despite the language barrier, the people manage to convey their desperation: "O Dhul-Qarnayn! Surely Ya'juj and Ma'juj are *mufsidun fi al-ard* — doing great mischief in the land. Shall we then pay you *kharj* in order that you might erect a barrier between us and them?"

Ibn Kathir relates, through Ibn Jurayj from 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas, that this *kharj* (tribute) meant a great reward: they wanted to collect money among themselves to give to him so that he would create a barrier between them and Ya'juj and Ma'juj. It is a moving picture — a people so weak that their only bargaining chip is pooled wealth, appealing to a passing king of evident power and justice.

Ibn Kathir notes that Dhul-Qarnayn answered "with kindness, righteousness and good intentions": the power and authority Allah had given him was better for him than what they had collected — he would build the barrier, and asked only for their labour and construction equipment. Ibn Kathir compares this to the words of Sulayman, peace be upon him: "Will you help me in wealth? What Allah has given me is better than that which He has given you!" (27:36). The full response belongs to the ayat that follow, but it is worth seeing here how the plea of ayah 94 is met: real power held as a trust from Allah does not sell protection to the desperate.

## Who are Ya'juj and Ma'juj?

The sources are emphatic on one point: Ya'juj and Ma'juj are human beings, among the progeny of Adam, peace be upon him. Ibn Kathir cites for this the hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs, in which Allah will say, "O Adam… send forth the group of Hellfire" — out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine to the Fire and one to Paradise — and which states plainly: "Among you are two nations who never come to anything but they overwhelm it with their huge numbers. (They are) Ya'juj and Ma'juj."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates the narration of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim, which carries the same scene with a further exchange: hearing that nine hundred and ninety-nine of every thousand are Hell-bound, the noble Sahabah were scared and asked, "Who from among us shall be the one bound to go to Paradise?" The Prophet ﷺ told them not to worry — of those nine hundred and ninety-nine, only one would be from among them, while, ratio-wise, a thousand would be from Ya'juj and Ma'juj. A narration of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar in the Mustadrak of al-Hakim adds that Allah divided mankind into ten parts, nine of them being Ya'juj and Ma'juj; Ibn Kathir, quoting such reports in al-Bidayah wa an-Nihayah, concludes that their numbers are significantly higher than the entire human population.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces their lineage further: since the Qur'an states that all humanity surviving after the Flood descends from Nuh, peace be upon him, they are of his progeny — historical narratives converge on their being descendants of his son Yafith, which is supported by a weak hadith as well. Importantly, it cautions that it is not necessary that these races were pinned down as a whole behind the wall of Dhul-Qarnayn; the name Ya'juj and Ma'juj applies only to the savage, uncivilized, blood-thirsty destroyers among them, not to the Turkic or Mongol peoples who became civilized.

## What the commentators add here — and where they draw the line

Because ayah 94 introduces these two nations, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses at this point to gather what the Sunnah establishes about them — while opening with an essential point of guidance: what must be believed is limited to what the Qur'an and Hadith state; much that circulates comes from untrustworthy Isra'ili narratives, and no article of faith depends on locating the wall on a map. The fuller discussion belongs with the ayat on the barrier itself; here only the essentials need be noted.

First, the long, sound hadith of an-Nawwas ibn Sam'an — reported in the Sahih of Muslim and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, in the recognized books of hadith, declared sound and authentic by the hadith experts — fixes the sequence of their final emergence: it comes only after the Dajjal (the false messiah) appears, 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon him, descends and kills him, and Allah then sends forth Ya'juj and Ma'juj, "against whom no two hands will dare fight," until He destroys them through the prayer of 'Isa and his companions. For this reason al-Qurtubi, seeing the Tatar invasions, would say only that they resembled Ya'juj and Ma'juj and could be their forerunners; and al-Alusi in Ruh al-Ma'ani strongly refuted equating any historical or modern power with the emergence itself, for that comes only after the descent of 'Isa, peace be upon him.

Second, in the hadith of Zainab bint Jahsh reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ awoke saying: "Alas for Arabia! Evil is drawing near. Today a part of the Wall of Ya'juj Ma'juj has opened up like this" — making a ring with the tips of his thumb and index finger. She asked, "Is our destruction possible even when we have righteous people among us?" He said, "Yes, it is — when evil abounds." A sobering principle sits inside the report: the presence of the righteous does not indemnify a society in which corruption has become general.

As for where the wall stands and whether it survives today, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān surveys the historians' candidates in the north — Darband (Bab al-Abwab) in Daghistan, which historians such as Mas'udi, Istakhri and Hamawi generally identified as the wall, and the wall of the Caucasus which Maulana Anwar Shah Kashmiri preferred — and records that the Qur'anic words about its end ("when the promise of my Lord comes," ayah 98) are, as al-Bahr al-Muhit notes, open to two readings, so that the wall may still exist or may already have crumbled. Both probabilities stand, and Allah knows reality best; what is not open to question, because the sound hadith of Muslim excludes it, is the claim that the great emergence has already taken place.

## What the passage leaves with the believer

Read as a whole, ayat 92–94 set up a meeting between three parties: overwhelming corruption (Ya'juj and Ma'juj, *mufsidun fi al-ard*), utter human weakness (a people who cannot even make themselves understood), and power held righteously (Dhul-Qarnayn). The weak do the one thing the weak can do — they seek help and offer what they have. And the passage's quiet teaching, completed in the ayat that follow, is that Allah positions His righteous servants precisely where such pleas can be answered, and that a believer entrusted with capability regards it as "that in which my Lord has established me" — a trust to be spent on shielding the vulnerable, not a commodity to be sold to them. As for Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the believer affirms what the Qur'an and the sound Sunnah affirm, leaves the geography to Allah's knowledge, and takes to heart the Prophet's ﷺ warning in the hadith of Zainab bint Jahsh: destruction draws near not when the righteous vanish, but when evil is allowed to abound.

passages.title: Building the iron barrier
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are the hinge of the Dhul-Qarnayn story. A threatened people have just offered him money to wall out Ya'juj and Ma'juj (Gog and Magog), and here he answers — refusing the payment, mobilising the people themselves, and raising a barrier of iron and molten copper between two mountains. What holds the passage together is a single movement from words to work: ayah 95 is the ethic of the builder, ayah 96 is the building itself.

## "What my Lord has established me in is better" (ayah 95)

The people had asked, as the preceding ayah records, "Shall we then pay you a tribute in order that you might erect a barrier between us and them?" Ibn Kathir reports, through Ibn Jurayj from 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas, that this meant a great reward — they wanted to collect money among themselves and hand it to him for the job.

Dhul-Qarnayn's reply, Ibn Kathir says, came "with kindness, righteousness and good intentions": *ma makkanni fihi Rabbi khayr* — "that in which my Lord has established me is better." The meaning, as Ibn Kathir explains it, is: the power and authority that Allah has given me is better for me than what you have collected. Notice where he locates his strength — not in armies or treasury, but in what "my Lord" has placed in his hands. The resources are Allah's grant; he is only their steward.

Ibn Kathir draws the natural parallel with Sulayman, peace be upon him, who said to the envoys: "Will you help me in wealth? What Allah has given me is better than that which He has given you!" (27:36). The two righteous kings speak with one voice: a ruler whom Allah has enriched does not sell protection to the desperate.

But the refusal of money is not a refusal of help. "So help me with strength (quwwah)" — meaning, as Ibn Kathir explains, with your labor and construction equipment. This is a telling exchange: he declines their gold but enlists their hands. The people are not left as passive clients paying a foreign strongman; they become partners in their own defense. He will direct the work; they will do it with him.

## The engineering of the barrier (ayah 96)

Ayah 96 compresses a massive construction project into a few commands, and each word repays attention.

**"Bring me zubar of iron."** *Zubar* is the plural of *zubrah* — pieces or chunks of something. This, Ibn Kathir notes, was the explanation of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah. The pieces were like bricks or blocks, and it was said each block weighed a Damascene qintar or more. So this is not sheet metal or fencing: it is masonry done in iron, block laid upon block.

**"Until, when he had filled up the gap between the two mountain-cliffs (al-sadafayn)."** The *sadafayn* are the two facing mountain-cliffs with the gap between them — the one breach through which the raiders poured. Ibn Kathir describes the method: he put the blocks on top of one another, starting at the bottom, until he reached the tops of the mountains, filling the width and the height of the gap. The scholars differed about the precise width and height, and the Qur'an does not give them; what matters is that the breach was sealed completely, flush with the mountains on either side.

**"Blow!"** In Ibn Kathir's words, he lit a fire until the whole thing was burning hot — the ayah, in the translation he comments on, says "when he had made them (red as) fire."

**"Bring me qitr to pour over it."** Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and al-Suddi said *qitr* is copper; some of them added that it was molten. Ibn Kathir points to the similar wording about the fount of qitr that Allah caused to flow for Sulayman in 34:12. Poured over the red-hot iron, the copper ran into the joints and fused the blocks into a single mass. The finished wall, Ibn Kathir says, resembled a striped cloak — bands of iron and copper.

The sequence matters. An iron wall of loose blocks can be dismantled; iron welded through fire and sealed in copper becomes one solid thing. And yet even this most permanent of structures is not treated as eternal: later in the same passage (ayah 98, which the commentators quoted here discuss), Dhul-Qarnayn says that "when the promise of my Lord" comes, Allah will level it to the ground. The wall's beginning lay in what Allah had established him in, and its end lies in Allah's promise — the builder claims neither.

## What the commentators attach to this passage

Because these ayat name Ya'juj and Ma'juj and describe the wall, the classical commentaries gather here a body of material about who they are and what became of the barrier. Maarif ul Quran opens that discussion with a principle worth keeping: much that circulates about this story comes from Isra'ili narratives and conjecture; what a Muslim must believe is limited to what the Qur'an and hadith state. No article of faith depends on locating the wall, and no ayah's meaning hinges on it. Within those limits, a brief summary of what the sources record:

**Who they are.** Ibn Kathir affirms that Ya'juj and Ma'juj are among the progeny of Adam, peace be upon him, citing the hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs in which Allah commands Adam on the Day of Rising to send forth the group of the Fire — nine hundred and ninety-nine of every thousand — and it is said: "Among you are two nations who never come to anything but they overwhelm it with their huge numbers: Ya'juj and Ma'juj." Maarif ul Quran adds that they are of the progeny of Nuh, peace be upon him — since the Qur'an states that all humanity after the Flood descends from him — and that historical reports converge on their being from the line of his son Yafith, though the hadith supporting that specific lineage is weak. Maarif also makes a careful distinction: it is not necessary that every tribe of these peoples was shut behind the wall. Some of their nations lived on the near side; what the barrier restrained were the savage, blood-thirsty destroyers among them — and it is to these alone that the name Ya'juj Ma'juj properly applies, not to the Turkic or Mongol peoples who became civilised.

**The wall in later reports.** Al-Bukhari and Muslim report from the Mother of the Believers Zainab bint Jahsh, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet ﷺ woke from sleep with his face red, saying: "La ilaha illa Allah. Alas for Arabia! Evil is drawing near. Today a part of the Wall of Ya'juj Ma'juj has opened up like this" — and he made a ring by joining the tips of his thumb and index finger. Zainab asked: "Ya Rasulallah, is our destruction possible even when we have righteous people among us?" He said: "Yes — when evil (khabath) abounds." The commentators read the opening of this hole either literally or figuratively — as a sign that the wall had weakened — but the moral of his ﷺ answer stands on its own: the presence of the righteous does not shield a society in which corruption has become pervasive.

The Musnad of Ahmad, Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah report from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, that Ya'juj Ma'juj dig at the wall every day until the light on the far side almost shows through, then leave saying they will finish tomorrow — and Allah restores it overnight; until, when Allah intends their release, they will say "if Allah wills, we shall go across it tomorrow," and find their digging preserved. The sources are candid about this narration's standing: Tirmidhi called it gharib (unfamiliar — known only through this route); Ibn Kathir judged that although its chain is good and strong, its ascription to the Prophet ﷺ is not supported by stronger sources, and that if it is in fact a narration from Ka'b al-Ahbar it is not worthy of trust; Ibn Hajar, on the other hand, reported it through further routes and did not doubt its ascription to the Prophet ﷺ. Maarif presents both sides rather than settling the matter.

**Where the wall is.** Ibn Khaldun, in the introduction to his history, places the "Wall of Alexander" in the Caucasus mountain range, between the Turkic Qipchaq and Circassian tribes on one side and Ya'juj Ma'juj on the other. He also quotes Ibn Khurdazbih's book of geography, which reports that the Abbasid caliph Wathiq Billah, disturbed by a dream that the wall had opened, sent his emissary Sallam on a fact-finding mission, who returned and described the wall's condition and features. Ibn Kathir too, in al-Bidayah wa an-Nihayah, confirms that Wathiq Billah sent an observer group which returned from its investigation, and records that the wall is made of iron with huge locked gates and lies toward the north-east. Maarif surveys four famous barrier-walls — the Great Wall of China, the Darband wall near Bukhara, the Darband (Bab al-Abwab) wall in Daghistan by the Caspian, and a wall at the Daryal Pass in the high Caucasus — and reasons that since the Qur'an indicates a northern location, the Great Wall of China is excluded; most historians (al-Mas'udi, al-Istakhri, al-Hamawi) favoured the Daghistan Darband, while Maulana Anwar Shah Kashmiri preferred the Caucasus wall.

**Does it still stand?** Maarif is deliberately even-handed. Against European geographers' claim that no such wall now blocks anyone, Kashmiri replied that unexplored regions remain and that the wall may even have merged into the mountains. But no decisive text (nass) of Qur'an or Sunnah requires the wall to remain standing until the end of time: "the promise of my Lord" in ayah 98 could mean the Day of Rising, or simply the appointed time of their release — al-Bahr al-Muhit records both readings. So the wall may have crumbled and some of these peoples may already have crossed over. What is fixed by the Sahih hadith of Muslim from an-Nawwas ibn Sam'an is only that their final, annihilating emergence — the one that is a sign of the Hour — comes after the descent of 'Isa, peace be upon him. To identify the Tatar invasions, or modern Russia and China, as that emergence is, in the words Maarif cites from al-Alusi, a flagrant error against the texts — though such upheavals may resemble it, as al-Qurtubi said of the Turks of his own era.

## What the passage teaches

Dhul-Qarnayn is the Qur'an's portrait of power held rightly, and these two ayat distil it. He attributes his strength to his Lord before he lifts a single block: "that in which my Lord has established me is better." He refuses to profit from the fear of the weak. He does not do for people what they can be enlisted to do for themselves — "help me with strength" turns a frightened population into a workforce. And he does the job properly: not a token fence, but iron fused with copper, built to outlast him. The pattern is set already here: capability from Allah, service without price, and thorough work in defense of the vulnerable.

passages.title: The barrier stands until the promise of the Lord
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are the closing scene of the story of Dhul-Qarnayn: the barrier against Ya'juj and Ma'juj (Gog and Magog) is finished, it proves impenetrable, and the man who built it turns away from his own work to speak of Allah's mercy and Allah's promise. What binds the ayat together is a single movement of thought — from the strength of the wall (ayah 97) to the humility of its builder and the certainty that even this wall will one day fall when "the promise of my Lord" comes (ayah 98). The barrier restrains them now; it will not restrain them forever.

## Ayah 97: a wall that could be neither climbed nor pierced

"And so the enemies could neither scale nor tunnel through it." Ibn Kathir draws attention to a subtlety in the Arabic that translation flattens: the verse uses two different forms of the same verb — *fa-mā isṭāʿū* ("they were not able") for scaling it, and the fuller *wa-mā istaṭāʿū* for digging through it. In his words, "varying forms of the verb are used here in the Arabic text to reflect the difficulty of the action referred to." The wall defeated them from above and from below: they could not climb over it, and they could not make a *naqb* — a breach or tunnel — through it. The two failures together are the Qur'an's way of saying the barrier was total.

## Ayah 98: "This is a mercy from my Lord"

Here is the moment that reveals Dhul-Qarnayn's character. The wall stands complete — and his first word is not about himself. Ibn Kathir makes two comments on this declaration. First, that Dhul-Qarnayn said it "after it was built" — the words come at the moment of completion, when a lesser man would have boasted. Second, that the mercy was "for the people, when he placed a barrier between them and Ya'juj and Ma'juj, to stop them from spreading evil and corruption on earth." The wall is not his monument; it is Allah's mercy, passing through his hands, for the protection of people from an enemy bent on corruption.

Then, in the same breath, he announces the wall's expiry: "but when the promise of my Lord comes, He shall make it *dakkāʾ*." Ibn Kathir opens up this striking word: the Arabs used *dakkāʾ* to describe a female camel whose back is flat, with no hump. The image is of something once towering being levelled until nothing protrudes. He connects it to Allah's words about the mountain: "So when his Lord appeared to the mountain, He made it *dakkan*" (7:143) — level to the ground. A wall of iron, and before it a mountain: whatever stands, stands only until Allah's decree arrives.

And the seal on the statement: "And the promise of my Lord is ever true" — meaning, as Ibn Kathir says, it will come to pass without a doubt. He then links this to the next ayah (99): on the day the barrier is breached, Ya'juj and Ma'juj will come out surging over mankind to destroy their wealth and property — As-Suddi said this refers to when they emerge upon the people — and all of this, Ibn Kathir notes, will happen before the Day of Resurrection and after the Dajjal.

## What is "the promise of my Lord"?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over this phrase, because scholars have read it in two ways, and the difference matters. Some took "the promise of my Lord" to mean the Day of Qiyamah itself, and built on this the claim that the wall must remain standing until the very end of time. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the words of the Qur'an are not definite and categorical about this. The phrase carries its own plain sense: the arrangement Dhul-Qarnayn made will not necessarily last forever; when Allah wills the passage to open, the wall will lie demolished — and that moment is whenever Allah has appointed it, not necessarily at the edge of the Hour. The commentary cites Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit, which states both possibilities openly: the promise may mean the Day of Qiyamah, or it may mean the time of the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes that neither reading can be ruled out by the texts: it cannot be declared with certainty that the wall has already disintegrated, nor that it must survive until Qiyamah. "Both probabilities exist. And Pure and High is Allah who knows reality best."

What *is* certain — because sound hadith establish it — is that the final, all-destroying onslaught of Ya'juj and Ma'juj has not yet happened and belongs to the end of time.

## The hole in the wall: the hadith of Zaynab bint Jahsh

The most arresting hadith the sources attach to these very ayat is recorded by both al-Bukhari and Muslim from Umm al-Mu'minin Zaynab bint Jahsh, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ woke from sleep with his face red, saying: "La ilaha illallah! Woe to the Arabs from the evil that has approached (them). Today a hole has been opened in the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj like this" — and he made a circle with his index finger and thumb. Zaynab asked: "O Messenger of Allah, will we be destroyed even though there will be righteous people among us?" He said: "Yes, if evil increases."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records — citing Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan — that this opening can be read in two ways: in the real sense, an actual hole of that measure appearing in the wall; or figuratively, indicating that the wall made by Dhul-Qarnayn had weakened, that the era of Ya'juj and Ma'juj's emergence had drawn nearer, and that its effects would show as decline for the Arabs. Either way, the Prophet's ﷺ answer to Zaynab carries the passage's sharpest practical warning: the presence of righteous people does not by itself avert destruction once evil (*khabath*) becomes abundant in a society.

## The daily digging: a hadith and how the scholars weighed it

The Musnad of Ahmad, Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah report from Abu Hurairah that the Prophet ﷺ said Ya'juj and Ma'juj dig at the iron wall every day until the light on the far side almost becomes visible; then they say they will dig through it the next day, and leave — and Allah makes it as strong as it was all over again. This will continue until Allah intends their release: then they will dig, reach the farthest limit, and say, "If Allah wills (*in shāʾ Allāh*), we shall go across it tomorrow" — and the next day they will find their work as they left it, and break through.

The sources are candid about this hadith's status, and the honesty is itself instructive. Tirmidhi called it *gharīb* — "Unfamiliar. We do not know it except from this source." Ibn Kathir judged its chain good and strong but held that its attribution to the Prophet ﷺ is not supported by stronger sources; if it is really a narration from Kaʿb al-Ahbar, he said, it is not worthy of trust — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes he declared it *maʿlūl* (defective despite an apparently correct chain). Hafiz Ibn Hajar, on the other hand, noted supporting routes through ʿAbd ibn Humaid and Ibn Hibban with some narrators of al-Bukhari's calibre, and did not doubt its being traceable to the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir also showed that, if it is accepted as the Prophet's ﷺ words, it does not contradict ayah 97: the digging would begin only when the hour of their emergence draws close, while the Qur'an's statement that no breach could be made refers to the wall as Dhul-Qarnayn made it — and the hadith itself makes clear that their hole never goes all the way through.

Ibn Hajar relays from Ibn al-Arabi that the hadith, if accepted, contains three divine signs: Allah never lets them think of digging in shifts around the clock, though their vast numbers would make that easy; He turns their minds away from devising means to scale over the wall; and for all those ages it never occurs to them to say "if Allah wills" — until the appointed time, when that one phrase, uttered at last, unlocks what ages of digging could not. Even the release of Ya'juj and Ma'juj happens not by their strength but by Allah's permission — the same lesson Dhul-Qarnayn spoke over the finished wall.

## Who are Ya'juj and Ma'juj? What the Sunnah establishes

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists on a method here: much of what circulates about Ya'juj and Ma'juj comes from Isra'ili narratives (reports of Jewish and Christian origin) and speculative history. What a Muslim must actually believe is only what the Qur'an and authentic hadith establish. From those sources, the commentary draws these conclusions.

**They are human beings**, progeny of Nuh (peace be upon him) like the rest of mankind — for the Qur'an states that all who survived the Flood are of his progeny — and historical narratives converge on their being of the line of his son Yafith. They are nations of men, not monsters. Nor is the name a blanket label for whole races: historians refer to them generally as Turks or Mongols, but Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful that the name Ya'juj Ma'juj applies only to the savage, uncivilized, blood-thirsty tyrants among them who remained untouched by civilization — it was these savage killers and destroyers whom the wall of Dhul-Qarnayn restrained, while other tribes of the same stock lived on this side of it.

**They are vast in number.** In a narration of Abu Saʿid al-Khudri in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ told his frightened Companions that of every thousand of Adam's progeny, nine hundred and ninety-nine are bound for the Fire — and then reassured them: of those nine hundred and ninety-nine, only one would be from among them, while, ratio-wise, a thousand would be from Ya'juj and Ma'juj. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes from the narrations that their number is several times that of the rest of mankind, at least ten to one.

**Their emergence has a fixed place in the sequence of the last days.** The long hadith of an-Nawwas ibn Samʿan — reported in the Sahih of Muslim and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, declared sound and authentic by the hadith experts — lays out the order: the Dajjal (the Antichrist) will appear and spread havoc; ʿIsa son of Maryam (peace be upon him) will descend — the hadith says he "will alight at the white tower in the eastern part of Dimashq (Damascus)" — and will kill the Dajjal at the gate of Ludd; and then Allah will reveal to ʿIsa that He is sending forth servants of His "against whom no two hands will dare fight" — Ya'juj and Ma'juj, seen hurtling down from every side. ʿIsa and the believers will take refuge on Mount Tur; the first wave of the hordes will drink Buhairah Tabariyyah (its lake) dry; and then, through the prayer of ʿIsa and his companions, Allah will destroy them all at once by an epidemic, wash the earth clean with rain, and open an era of such blessing that one pomegranate will suffice as food for a group of people. Notably, this same hadith is where the Prophet ﷺ taught that whoever encounters the Dajjal should recite the initial verses of Surah al-Kahf — the very surah we are reading — as protection against him.

Because this sequence is fixed by sound hadith, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — citing ʿAllamah Alusi's Ruh al-Maʿani — rules out identifying the Tatar invasions of the sixth Islamic century, or modern Russia, China or Europe, as *the* emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj: to Alusi this is a flagrant error that opposes the textual authority of hadith, since the true emergence comes only after the Dajjal appears and ʿIsa (peace be upon him) descends and kills him. At most, said al-Qurtubi and Alusi, such upheavals *resemble* that final havoc, or are its forerunners.

## Where is the wall? A question faith does not depend on

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic on a point of method: no Islamic article of faith depends on locating the wall, and the understanding of these ayat does not hinge on it. Scholars discussed geography only to answer objectors and provide additional insight. In summary: several great defensive walls exist — the Great Wall of China (which no one identifies as Dhul-Qarnayn's wall: it lies in the Far East, whereas the Qur'an indicates a northern location), a wall at Darband near Bukhara and Tirmidh, the famous wall at Darband (Bab al-Abwab) in Daghistan by the Caspian Sea, and a wall in the Caucasus at the Daryal Pass. Historians such as Masʿudi, Istakhri and Hamawi generally favoured the Daghistan wall; Maulana Anwar Shah Kashmiri preferred the Caucasus wall; and much confusion arose simply because two different sites share the name "Darband." Ibn Khaldun located the wall in the Caucasus range in the prolegomena of his history, and both he and Ibn Kathir (in al-Bidayah wa an-Nihayah) record that the Abbasid caliph Wathiq Billah sent an expedition that returned having investigated the wall — described as made of iron with huge locked gates, towards the north-east.

And if European geographers say no such wall can now be found, Kashmiri replied that their own admissions of unexplored forests, rivers and islands rob the claim of weight — and that the wall, though present, may even have taken the form of a mountain through mountains crumbling and joining together. The texts allow that the wall may already have disintegrated and that some of these peoples may already have crossed over; what they do not allow is any claim that the final onslaught has already come.

## Living these ayat

Two postures emerge from this passage. The first is Dhul-Qarnayn's: at the moment of achievement, say "this is a mercy from my Lord" — attribute the accomplishment to Allah, use strength to shield people from evil and corruption, and hold every human construction lightly, knowing it stands only until Allah's promise arrives, "and the promise of my Lord is ever true." The second is the Prophet's ﷺ warning to Zaynab: a society is not saved by the mere existence of righteous people in it, but destroyed when evil increases — so the believer's task is not passive righteousness but resisting the spread of corruption. And woven through both is the quiet lesson of *in shāʾ Allāh*: the barrier holds, and falls, by Allah's will alone.

passages.title: The surge, the trumpet, and Hell displayed
passages.tafsir:
## The surge, the trumpet, and Hell displayed

The story of Dhul-Qarnayn's barrier has just ended with his own words — "This is a mercy from my Lord, but when the promise of my Lord comes, He shall level it to the ground" (ayah 98) — and Ibn Kathir notes that this promise "will come to pass without a doubt." The ayat before us now show that promise arriving. In four swift ayat we move from the surge when the barrier gives way (ayah 99), to the trumpet and the universal gathering (end of ayah 99), to Hell brought out into plain view (ayah 100), to the verdict on why its people deserved it (ayat 101–102).

## Ayah 99 — the surge: who is surging?

"On that Day, We will let them surge like waves over one another." The verb *yamūju* is the language of the sea — a heaving, wave-like churning of masses.

The commentators discuss who "them" refers to, and the two great sources here read it differently:

- **Ibn Kathir** takes the pronoun to mean **mankind**: on the day the barrier is breached, Ya'juj and Ma'juj (Gog and Magog) will come out "surging over mankind to destroy their wealth and property." He cites the early authority **As-Suddi**: "That is when they emerge upon the people."
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** holds it is obvious that the pronoun refers to **Ya'juj and Ma'juj themselves**: when the passage finally lies open, they will hasten their way "from the hilly heights down to the ground," surging over one another — while noting that commentators have suggested other possibilities as well.

Both readings paint the same scene from different angles: a barrier that stood for ages suddenly gives way, and an unstoppable mass of people crashes like surf. Ibn Kathir fixes the timing precisely: all of this happens **before the Day of Resurrection and after the Dajjal**, and he connects it to Allah's words elsewhere: "Until, when Ya'juj and Ma'juj are let loose, and they swoop down from every Hadab. And the true promise shall draw near…" (21:96–97).

**A warning given in the Prophet's ﷺ own lifetime.** Ibn Kathir records — via Imam Ahmad, and he notes it is a sahih hadith that both al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded — that Zaynab bint Jahsh, the Prophet's ﷺ wife, said he woke from sleep red in the face, saying: "Lā ilāha illallāh! Woe to the Arabs from the evil that has approached (them). Today a hole has been opened in the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj like this" — and he made a circle with his index finger and thumb. Zaynab asked: "O Messenger of Allah, will we be destroyed even though there will be righteous people among us?" He said: "**Yes, if evil increases.**"

## The trumpet and the gathering

The same ayah then leaps past the breach to the event it heralds: "and the Trumpet will be blown, and We shall collect them all together."

**The Sūr**, Ibn Kathir explains from the hadith, is a **horn** that is blown into, and the one who will blow it is the angel **Isrāfīl**, peace be upon him. Ibn Kathir also relates a hadith narrated from ʿAtiyah, from Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Saʿid, and attributed to the Prophet ﷺ: "How can I relax when the one with the Horn has put the Horn in his mouth and has knelt down, listening out for the command to be given to him?" The Companions asked what they should say, and he taught them: "**Say: Allah is Sufficient for us and the best Disposer of affairs, in Allah have we put our trust** (Hasbunā Allāhu wa niʿma al-wakīl, ʿalā Allāhi tawakkalnā)." The horn is already at the angel's lips — and the believer's response to that terrifying nearness is not panic but tawakkul, entrusting the matter to Allah.

**Who is gathered?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out a subtle shift in the pronouns: while "them surging" refers to Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the "them" of "We shall gather them together" (*fa-jamaʿnāhum*) widens out to **the whole of creation — human beings and the jinn** — everyone who was obligated with the precepts of the Sharīʿah (in the scholars' term, *mukallaf*, morally accountable), gathered together on the plains of the Resurrection (*al-hashr*). Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as: "We shall bring them all together for Reckoning," and seals the point with parallel ayat: "Verily, those of old, and those of later times. All will surely be gathered together for appointed meeting of a known Day" (56:49–50), and from this very sūrah, "We shall gather them all together so as to leave not one of them behind" (18:47). No generation is too early, no individual too obscure.

## Ayah 100 — Hell brought out to be seen

"On that Day We will display Hell clearly for the disbelievers." Ibn Kathir explains the purpose of this display: Allah will bring Hell forth **for them to see its punishment and torment before they enter it — to intensify their distress and grief**. The punishment begins with the sight of the punishment.

How is a thing like Hell "displayed"? The Sunnah gives the scene its scale. In **Sahih Muslim** it is recorded that Ibn Masʿūd said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "**Hell will be brought forth on the Day of Resurrection, pulled by means of seventy thousand reins, each of which will be held by seventy thousand angels.**" A created terror so immense that it must itself be restrained, dragged into view before the assembled creation.

## Ayah 101 — the covering they chose

Then Allah describes who these disbelievers are: "those whose eyes had been under a covering (*ghitāʼ*) from My Reminder, and they could not bear to hear it."

Notice what the ayah does **not** say — it does not say they were created blind to the truth. Ibn Kathir explains the covering as their own doing: **"they neglected it, turning a blind eye and a deaf ear to it, refusing to accept guidance and follow the truth."** The eyes worked; they were simply kept wrapped away from the Reminder — Allah's revelation and remembrance. And "they could not bear to hear" means, in Ibn Kathir's words, that they did not understand the commands and prohibitions of Allah. Ibn Kathir illuminates this with a parallel ayah: "Whosoever turns away blindly from the remembrance of the Most Gracious, We appoint for him a Shaytan to be a companion for him" (43:36) — willful blindness is not a neutral state; it attracts a darker companionship.

There is a piercing symmetry across ayat 100 and 101: they refused to *see* the Reminder in this world, so in the next world they are made to *see* Hell, plainly, before they ever enter it.

## Ayah 102 — the false protectors

The passage closes with a question: "Do the disbelievers think they can take My servants as *awliyāʼ* — protectors — besides Me?"

**What the question really asks.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit, explains that the sentence contains an elision (*hadhf* — words understood but left unsaid): the full sense is, "Do these disbelievers, who have taken My servants instead of Me as objects of worship and dispensers of their affairs, think that this makeshift arrangement will **benefit** them?" It is an interrogative of negation and disapproval: such thinking is wrong, a mark of ignorance. Ibn Kathir reads it the same way — "do they think that this is right for them and that it is going to benefit them?" — and answers it with Allah's words: "Nay, but they will deny their worship of them, and become opponents to them" (19:82). The very "protectors" will disown their worshippers on that Day.

**Who are "My servants"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān surveys the scholars' views:

- The **weightier view**, per al-Bahr al-Muhit and other tafsirs: the **angels and the particular prophets** whom people wrongly worshipped — some Arabs worshipped angels; the Jews ascribed partnership to Allah in respect of ʿUzair, and the Christians in respect of ʿĪsā, peace be upon them both.
- Some commentators took "My servants" to mean the **shaytans**, so the disbelievers meant are those who worship the jinn and shaytans.
- Others took it in the **general sense** of anything created and under Allah's mastery — inclusive of all false objects of worship, idols, fire, and stars; Maulana Ashraf ʿAli Thanavi referred to this reading, explaining "servants" as subjects.

The irony is built into the word itself: they took Allah's *ʿibād* — His own servants — as substitutes for Him.

**The key word *awliyāʼ*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *waliyy* (plural *awliyāʼ*) carries several meanings in Arabic, and here it means **one who gets things done, resolves matters, and fulfills needs — which is the particular attribute of the true object of worship**. To take someone as a walī in this sense is precisely to take him as an object of worship. The ayah then delivers the verdict: far from being sheltered by these imagined protectors, "We have prepared Hell as an entertainment for the disbelievers" — Ibn Kathir: Allah has prepared Hell as their abode on the Day of Resurrection. The only reception awaiting that false arrangement is the Fire.

## Living this passage

Two responses are written into the sources themselves. First, the Prophet ﷺ answered Zaynab's question — can destruction come while the righteous still live among us? — with "Yes, if evil increases": the presence of righteous people alone does not avert destruction when evil abounds. Second, when the Companions felt the terror of the horn already at the angel's lips, the Prophet ﷺ gave them words, not despair: *Hasbunā Allāhu wa niʿma al-wakīl* — "Allah is Sufficient for us and the best Disposer of affairs, in Allah have we put our trust." And the covering of ayah 101 stands as the passage's quiet warning: the blindness that ends before a displayed Hell begins as a daily, chosen turning of the eyes away from the Reminder.

passages.title: The greatest losers versus the people of Firdaws
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the closing verdict of Sūrat al-Kahf's long meditation on deeds and their worth. It sets two destinies side by side in the starkest possible contrast: the people whose lifetime of effort evaporates into nothing on the Day of Resurrection (ayat 103–106), and the believers who are welcomed as honoured guests into al-Firdaws, the highest garden of Paradise, never wishing to leave (ayat 107–108). What binds the six ayat together is a single question — what makes a deed *count*? — answered first negatively, then positively.

## "Shall We tell you the greatest losers?"

Ayah 103 opens with a question Allah commands the Prophet ﷺ to pose: *"Shall We tell you the greatest losers in respect of their deeds?"* The rhetorical form matters. These are not people who did nothing; the shock the ayah builds toward is that they were *busy*. Ayah 104 delivers it: their efforts were wasted in this life *"while they thought that they were acquiring good by their deeds."* Ibn Kathir explains: they did deeds that do not count — deeds not in accordance with the way prescribed and accepted by Allah — while believing all along that their works rested on a solid basis and were accepted and loved.

This is loss of a uniquely painful kind: not the loss of the idle, but of the earnest and self-assured. Ibn Kathir connects it to other Qur'anic images of the same fate — faces on that Day "humiliated, labouring, weary" as they enter the Fire (88:2–4); deeds turned into "scattered floating particles of dust" (25:23); and the disbeliever's works as "a mirage in a desert — the thirsty one thinks it to be water, until he comes up to it, he finds it to be nothing" (24:39). The mirage image is the key to the whole passage: the deception is not discovered until the moment of greatest need.

## Who are they? The Companions' discussion

Ibn Kathir records a striking exchange preserved in al-Bukhari. Muṣʿab asked his father, Saʿd bin Abi Waqqas, about this ayah: are "the greatest losers" the Haruriyyah? Saʿd answered: "No, they are the Jews and Christians. As for the Jews, they disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ, and as for the Christians, they disbelieved in Paradise and said that there is no food or drink there; and the Haruriyyah are those who break Allah's covenant after ratifying it." Saʿd used to call the Haruriyyah *al-Fasiqin*, the corrupt. Yet ʿAli bin Abi Talib himself, along with Ad-Dahhak and others, did say of this ayah, "They are the Haruriyyah."

Ibn Kathir resolves the apparent disagreement decisively: the ayah was not revealed about any of these groups in particular. It came down in Makkah — before the Qur'an ever addressed the Jews and Christians, and before the Khawarij existed at all. So the Companions were naming *examples*, not the referent. The ayah is general: it covers "everyone who worships Allah in a way that is not acceptable, thinking that he is right in doing that and that his deeds will be accepted, but he is mistaken and his deeds will be rejected."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Qurtubi, sharpens the diagnosis: deeds are ruined in this way by two things. One, **corruption in belief** — a person whose faith itself is not sound will find even painstaking good works useless in the Hereafter. Two, **hypocrisy** — acting for the pleasure of the created rather than for Allah leaves a deed deprived of its reward. It is in this general sense that some Companions applied the ayah to the Kharijites, and some commentators to the Muʿtazilah, the Rawafid and other groups that strayed. At the same time, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Mazhari prefer the view that the ones *primarily* meant are the particular disbelievers described in ayah 105 — those who deny Allah's signs, the Last Day and the Reckoning — since the ayah itself goes on to define them; yet all whose deeds are wasted by corrupt belief remain touched by its general sense.

## The scale that registers nothing

Ayah 105 names the root: *"It is they who reject the signs of their Lord and their meeting with Him."* Ibn Kathir unpacks both halves — they denied the proofs Allah established in this world of His Oneness and of the truth of His Messengers, and they denied the Hereafter. Then comes the sentence that gives the passage its terror: *"on the Day of Resurrection, We shall assign no weight for them."* Ibn Kathir: "We will not make their Balance heavy, because it is empty of any goodness." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that their deeds may look imposing from the outside, but on the balance of reckoning they register nothing, because *kufr* (disbelief) and *shirk* (ascribing partners to Allah) have hollowed them out.

Both commentaries cite the hadith that the Prophet ﷺ himself attached to this very ayah. Al-Bukhari — and Muslim also — record from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A huge fat man will come forward on the Day of Resurrection and he will weigh no more than the wing of a gnat to Allah." Then he said: "Recite, if you wish: *and on the Day of Resurrection, We shall assign no weight for them*." A man of great worldly substance — and the scale of Allah does not stir. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also relays the saying of Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, cited by al-Qurtubi: on the Day of Qiyamah, deeds as big as the mountains of Tihamah will be brought in — and carry no weight on the balance of justice.

Ayah 106 seals the sentence: Hell is their recompense — and note the two grounds the ayah gives: *because they disbelieved*, and because *they took My Ayat and My Messengers for jest*. Ibn Kathir observes that they did not merely reject the truth; they mocked it, treating Allah's signs and Messengers as a joke — disbelief in its worst form.

## The people of Firdaws

Then the passage pivots. Ayah 107: *"Indeed, those who believe and do good will have the Gardens of al-Firdaws"* — the two conditions, faith and righteous deeds, answering exactly the two failures above (corrupt belief, worthless works). Ibn Kathir: these are Allah's blessed servants who believed in Allah and His Messengers and accepted as truth what the Messengers brought.

What is al-Firdaws? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word as a verdant valley full of fruits and flowers, used here of Paradise — noting that scholars differed even over the word's origin, whether Arabic or borrowed (Persian, Greco-Roman or Syriac). Ibn Kathir gathers the early authorities: Abu Umamah said, "Al-Firdaws is the centre of Paradise"; Qatadah said, "Al-Firdaws is a hill in Paradise, at its centre, the best of it" — a description also narrated from Samurah and attributed to the Prophet ﷺ, all recorded by Ibn Jarir. And in the Sahih is the Prophet's ﷺ counsel: "If you ask Allah for Paradise, then ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the highest part of Paradise, in the middle of Paradise, and from it spring the rivers of Paradise." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same hadith from the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim with the addition that above al-Firdaws is the Throne of the Rahman. The practical instruction is remarkable: when you ask, do not ask small. Ask for the summit.

One small word in ayah 107 carries the warmth of the scene: *nuzulan*. Ibn Kathir explains it as hospitality — the Gardens are offered to them the way a host lays out entertainment for an honoured guest. Against the humiliated labourers of ayah 104 stands a people *received*.

## Forever — and never bored

Ayah 108 closes the surah's contrast with a subtle psychological truth: *"where they will be forever, never desiring anywhere else"* (*la yabghuna ʿanha hiwala* — they will not seek any removal or change from it). Both commentaries pause here, because the ayah anticipates a doubt. Human beings, by nature, tire of any one place; we itch to move on. Would eternity in even the most beautiful garden not eventually feel like confinement? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers from the ayah itself: to measure Jannah by the analogy of worldly places is sheer ignorance. Once a person enters, everything he ever saw and lived in the mortal world becomes trifling beside the bliss and beauty of Jannah — so no one would ever even think of leaving. Ibn Kathir reads the phrase the same way: it tells us "how much they love and desire it" — despite an eternal stay, they will never choose to change or move.

## Holding the two panels together

Read as one unit, the passage teaches that deeds are weighed, not counted. Effort alone guarantees nothing: sincerity of belief and conformity to what Allah has prescribed are what give a deed its weight, and their absence can turn a mountain of works into a mirage. The most sobering note — drawn out by Ibn Kathir's insistence that the ayah is general — is that the greatest losers *thought they were doing well*. That is why the passage matters to a believer and not only as a description of others: it presses each reader to examine both the soundness of what he believes and the sincerity of why he acts. And it ends not with fear but with an invitation and a target: faith joined to righteous deeds, and a prayer the Prophet ﷺ taught us to make specific — ask Allah for al-Firdaws itself, the highest and best of Paradise, a home its people will never once wish to trade.

passages.title: Boundless divine words and the Prophet's humanity
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are the seal of Surah al-Kahf. Ayah 109 lifts the eyes upward: the Words of Allah are so boundless that every ocean turned to ink would run dry before they could be written. Ayah 110 then brings the gaze back down to earth: the man who delivers those Words is "only a man like you" — and the only way to meet the Lord of those infinite Words is a deed done purely for Him, in the way His Messenger ﷺ taught. Held together, the pair closes the surah with the two poles of the whole religion: the limitless majesty of Allah, and the plain, humble path by which a limited human being reaches Him.

## Ayah 109: if the sea were ink

Ibn Kathir unfolds the image simply: Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ to say that if the water of the sea were ink for a pen to write down the words, wisdom and signs of Allah, the sea would run dry before it all could be written down. And the phrase "even if We brought like it for its aid" means another sea, then another, and so on — additional seas brought in for the writing — and still the Words of Allah would never run out.

Ibn Kathir points to the parallel ayah in Surah Luqman: "And if all the trees on the earth were pens and the sea (were ink), with seven seas behind it to increase it, yet the Words of Allah would not be exhausted. Verily, Allah is All-Mighty, All-Wise" (31:27). Even then, he says, the pens would be broken and the water of the sea would run dry, and the Words of Allah would remain, for nothing can outlast them.

**Why this was revealed.** Ibn Kathir records the saying of the early authority ar-Rabi' bin Anas: "The parable of the knowledge of all of mankind, in comparison to the knowledge of Allah, is that of a drop of water in comparison to all of the oceans." It was in that connection, he says, that Allah revealed this ayah.

Ibn Kathir draws the lesson to its proper end: no one can comprehend the greatness of Allah or praise Him as He deserves to be praised, except the One Who praises Himself. **Our Lord is as He says He is, and He is beyond what we can say.** Ibn Kathir adds a final comparison in the same spirit of scale: the blessings of this world, from its beginning to its end, are to the blessings of the Hereafter like a mustard seed compared to the entire world.

## Ayah 110: "I am only a man like you"

Immediately after the ayah of infinite Words comes the ayah of the finite messenger. Ibn Kathir explains: Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ to say to the idolators who reject his message, "I am only a man like you" — and this very humanity is the proof of his truthfulness. Whoever claims he is lying, let him bring something like what he has brought. He did not know the Unseen; the matters of the past they asked him about and he told them about — the story of the people of the Cave and of Dhul-Qarnayn, stories which are true — he knew none of it except what Allah made known to him. A mere man producing such knowledge can only be a man receiving revelation. And the content of that revelation is one sentence: that your ilāh — the One you worship — is Allah alone, One, with no partner or associate.

The ayah then turns from creed to conduct: "So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord" — that is, as Ibn Kathir explains, whoever hopes for a good reward and recompense — "let him work righteousness and associate none as a partner in the worship of his Lord."

**The two conditions of an accepted deed.** Ibn Kathir reads the closing clause as a complete definition. "Let him work righteousness" means acting in accordance with the prescribed laws of Allah; "and associate none in the worship of his Lord" means seeking the pleasure of Allah alone. These, he says, are the two basic features of acceptable deeds: their intent is for the sake of Allah alone, and they are done in accordance with the way of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Sincerity without conformity fails; conformity without sincerity fails. The surah that began with revelation ends by telling the reader exactly how to respond to it.

## The hidden shirk: why this ayah came down

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the shirk prohibited at the end of this ayah, according to the hadith reports on its revelation, is not only the open idolatry of the pagans but the *hidden* shirk — riyāʼ, showing off: doing a deed of worship with an eye on people's admiration.

Several occasions of revelation are transmitted:

- Imam Hakim reports in al-Mustadrak, from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas — grading it sound on the criterion of al-Bukhari and Muslim — that one of the Muslims used to carry out jihad in the way of Allah, while also wishing that his soldiering and bravery be recognized and appreciated by people. The verse was revealed about him, teaching that one gets no reward by having such an intention in jihad.
- Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Abi al-Dunya report in Kitab al-Ikhlas, from Tawus, that a Companion said to the Prophet ﷺ: when I worship or do a righteous deed, my aim is nothing but the pleasure of Allah — yet I also wish that people would see me doing it. The Prophet ﷺ kept silent until this verse was revealed.
- In Abu Nuʿaym and the history of Ibn ʿAsakir, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas: whenever the Companion Jundub ibn Zuhayr prayed, fasted or gave charity and saw people admiring him, he felt pleased and would increase those deeds. Thereupon this verse was revealed.

The gist, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it: a deed may be for Allah, but if a selfish motive of name, fame and recognition becomes attached to it, that attachment is a kind of hidden shirk — something that makes the deed go to waste, and can even become harmful.

## When praise is not riyāʼ

Yet other authentic hadiths seem, at first sight, to point the other way, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets them side by side:

- Tirmidhi reports from Abu Hurairah that he asked the Prophet ﷺ: sometimes I am praying inside my house and someone comes upon me, and I am pleased that he saw me in that state — is that riyāʼ? The Prophet ﷺ answered: "O Abu Hurairah, may Allah have mercy on you. Then you get two rewards: one for the deed you were already doing in secret, and the other for what you did openly after the coming of that person."
- In the Sahih of Muslim, from Abu Dharr al-Ghifari: the Prophet ﷺ was asked about a person who does a good deed and then hears people praising it. He said, "This is instant good news for the believer" — a sign that the deed was accepted and Allah has caused His servants to praise it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Tafsir Mazhari's reconciliation. The revelation narrations describe the case where a person *mixes into his intention* the desire to please people or earn a name — to the point that praise makes him increase the deed. That is riyāʼ and hidden shirk. The Tirmidhi and Muslim narrations describe a different case: the person acted for Allah alone, with no inclination toward publicity, and then Allah in His grace gave him fame by making people praise him. That has nothing to do with showing off; it is glad tidings arriving early. The dividing line is not whether people see you, but what you were seeking when you acted.

## Warnings, and a shield

The hadith warnings on riyāʼ are stern, and the sources for this ayah gather several:

- Imam Ahmad recorded that Mahmud bin Labid said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What I fear the most for you is the small shirk." They asked what the small shirk was, and he said: "Showing off (ar-riyāʼ). Allah will say on the Day of Resurrection, when the people are rewarded or punished for their deeds: go to the one for whom you were showing off in the world and see if you will find any reward with him."
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that after reporting this hadith of Mahmud ibn Labid in Shuʿab al-Iman, al-Baihaqi also reported the remarks: on the day of Qiyamah, when Allah Taʿala will reward His servants for their deeds, He will ask the practitioners of riyāʼ to go for their rewards to those they wanted to impress with their deeds, and find out whether or not they have any for them.
- Imam Ahmad also recorded, from the Companion Abu Saʿid bin Abi Fadalah al-Ansari, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah will gather the first and the last on the Day of Resurrection, the Day concerning which there is no doubt. A voice will call out: whoever used to associate anyone with Allah in the deeds which he did, let him seek his reward from someone other than Allah, for Allah is the least in need of any partner or associate." It was also recorded by at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah.
- Muslim narrates from Abu Hurairah that the Prophet ﷺ said Allah Taʿala says: "I am free and above associating with those associated with Me. Whoever does a good deed and then associates in it someone else with Me, I leave the entire deed for the one associated" — and in another narration, "I withdraw from that deed, making it exclusive for the person associated with Me."
- Ahmad narrates in Shuʿab al-Iman, from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: whoever does a good deed to earn a fair name among people, Allah deals with him in a manner that he is disgraced before them.

**What sincerity looks like.** Tafsir al-Qurtubi relates that Hasan al-Basri, asked about ikhlās (unalloyed sincerity — the opposite of riyāʼ) and riyāʼ, said: ikhlās requires that you *like* your good deeds to remain hidden and *dislike* your bad deeds remaining hidden; and if Allah then discloses your deeds before people, you say, "O Allah, all this is Your grace and favour, not the outcome of my deed and effort."

**A daily protection.** Tirmidhi reports from Abu Bakr that the Prophet ﷺ once described shirk as being "right there in you, more stealthily than the soundless movement of an ant," and then taught a duʿāʼ which, said three times every day, keeps one safe against all shirk, major and minor: *Allāhumma innī aʿūdhu bika an ushrika bika wa ana aʿlam, wa astaghfiruka limā lā aʿlam* — "O Allah, I seek refuge with You lest I associate a partner with You while I know, and I seek forgiveness from You for what I do not know." The prayer itself acknowledges that shirk can hide from its own doer: it covers both the shirk we can see in ourselves and the shirk we cannot.

## The blessings of these closing verses

Because these are the final ayat of al-Kahf, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with the merits attached to the surah's beginning and end:

- Abu al-Dardaʼ reports that the Prophet ﷺ said whoever remembers to recite the first ten verses of Surah al-Kahf will remain safe against the fitnah of Dajjal (reported by Muslim, Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Nasaʼi); and within this narration, words to the effect that whoever remembers the *last* ten verses will likewise remain safe from Dajjal's trial (Ahmad, Muslim and al-Nasaʼi).
- According to a narration of Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said: whoever recites the opening and closing verses of the surah will have light from his feet to his head, and whoever recites the whole surah will have light from the ground to the sky (Ibn al-Sunni, and Ahmad in his Musnad).
- As narrated by Abu Saʿid, the Prophet ﷺ said: whoever recites Surah al-Kahf in full on the day of Jumuʿah will have light until the next Jumuʿah (reported and declared Sahih by al-Hakim, and by al-Baihaqi in al-Daʿawat).

There is even a practical use of these very two ayat. Someone told ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas that he resolved to wake in the later part of the night to pray but sleep would overtake him. Ibn ʿAbbas told him: recite the last verses of Surah al-Kahf — from "If the sea were ink" (109) to the end (110) — before you sleep, and Allah will wake you at the time you intend (reported by ath-Thaʿalibi). And in the Musnad of al-Darimi, Zirr ibn Hubaish told ʿAbdah the same, and ʿAbdah said: "We have tried this repeatedly. It happens just like that."

## Living the ending

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān leaves the reader with the counsel of Ibn al-ʿArabi's teacher, Turtushi, quoted via al-Qurtubi: do not let the hours of your dear life pass away in rivalry with contemporaries and socializing with friends — watch out, for Allah has concluded His statement on this very verse: "So the one who hopes to meet his Lord must do righteous deeds and must not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord."

That is the summary of the surah, and of a believing life. In ayah 109 you learn Who your Lord is — the One whose Words no ocean can contain. In ayah 110 you learn what He asks of you — not oceans, but one thing done two ways: a deed that follows the Messenger ﷺ, offered to no audience but Allah. The hope of meeting Him is real; the road to it is sincerity so complete that even the ant-quiet whisper of showing off is swept out of the heart.
